The university's big, but I don't have any friends.

notes.text: けど joins two sentences that pull different ways. Friends say けど; だけど after a noun.
が for "but" comes after です or ます more often than after the plain form. At the end of a sentence, けど leaves the rest unsaid, which softens it.

grammar.title: ～よう / ～おう
grammar.summary: The volitional form is a casual "let's": 行こう, let's go. Said about yourself, it's what you've decided: 歌おう, I'll sing.
grammar.body:
みんなで行こう！
一緒に歌おう！

notes.text: う verbs change their last sound to the お row and add う: 行く, 行こう; 歌う, 歌おう. る verbs swap る for よう: 食べる, 食べよう.
する and 来る have their own: しよう, 来よう. Among friends it's how you suggest anything; ～ましょう is the polite version.

grammar.title: ～と思う / ～と
grammar.summary: と思う after a plain sentence says what you think: 歌うと思う, I think I'll sing. The same と quotes what someone said: 「来年は歌う」と言った.
grammar.body:
次は歌うと思う。
ユキの歌は、いいと思う。
ユキは「来年は歌う」と言った。
translations: I think I'll sing next time.
I think Yuki's songs are good.

notes.text: What you think comes first, in the plain form, then と思う. With strangers it's と思います.
と also marks the words of a quote, before 言う and verbs like it. The quote can be the exact words, in 「」, or put in your own.

grammar.title: ～って / ～という
grammar.summary: って is a casual と言う: 歌うって, says she's singing. という names something: 『雪』という曲, a song called "Snow".
grammar.body:
ユキが歌うって？
僕が『ユキさんが歌う』って書いた。
『雪』という曲です。

notes.text: って quotes what someone said or wrote, and the verb after it often drops: 歌うって (言った). Said with a rise, it checks what you heard.
という (と plus 言う) puts a name or a description in front of a noun: what it's called.

grammar.title: かな / かも
grammar.summary: かな at the end of a sentence wonders out loud: 大丈夫かな, will it be okay, I wonder. かも (かもしれない) says it might be so: 出ないかも, it might not come out.
grammar.body:
私、大丈夫かな。
声が出ないかも。
translations: Will I be okay, I wonder.
My voice might not come out.

notes.text: かな is か (a question) and な (to yourself): a question you don't expect anyone to answer. It's casual.
かも is short for かもしれない, "it might be", about half sure. It goes after the plain form, or straight after a noun: 無理かも, maybe not.

grammar.title: ～える / ～られる
grammar.summary: The potential form says what you can do: 歌う (sing), 歌える (can sing); 出る (go out, take part), 出られる (can take part).
grammar.body:
新しいバンドも、出られる？
ユキさん、歌えるじゃん！
明日は行けない。

notes.text: う verbs change their last sound to the え row and add る: 行く, 行ける; 歌う, 歌える. る verbs take られる: 出る, 出られる. In speech that's often just れる: 出れる.
The new verb changes like a る verb: 行けない (can't go), 歌えた (could sing). 来る becomes 来れる, and する becomes できる, which you know already.

grammar.title: ～たら
grammar.summary: ら on a verb's past form says "if" or "when": 勝ったら, if we win. It's the everyday way to say "if".
grammar.body:
もし勝ったら、どうする？
雨が降ったら、どうする？
負けたら、また来年。
練習が終わったら、ラーメン食べよう。
translations: What do we do if we win?
If we lose, there's next year.
Let's have ramen once practice is over.

notes.text: Take the plain past and add ら: 勝った, 勝ったら; 降った, 降ったら. Then say what happens. もし (if) in front is optional; it flags early that an "if" is coming.
It works on any past form: 負けなかったら (if we don't lose), 出られたら (if we can get in), 暑かったら (if it's hot), 雨だったら (if it's rain).
For something sure to happen, たら means "when" or "once": 終わったら, when it's over.

grammar.title: ～なきゃ / ～なくてもいい
grammar.summary: なきゃいけない or なくちゃ on a verb's ない stem says you have to: 練習しなくちゃ, I have to practise. なくてもいい says you don't: 緊張しなくてもいい, no need to be nervous.
grammar.body:
練習しなくちゃ。
動画を送らなきゃいけない。
新しい曲じゃなくてもいい。
translations: We have to send a video.
It doesn't have to be a new song.

notes.text: Take the ない form and swap ない for なくちゃ: 練習しない, 練習しなくちゃ. It's short for なくては (いけない): "if I don't, it won't do".
なきゃ is short for なければ, "if not", and does the same job. Friends often drop the いけない. In writing and formal talk it's the whole なければならない.
なくてもいい is the other way round: even not doing it is fine. After a noun it's じゃなくてもいい.

grammar.title: ～くなる / ～になる / ～く
grammar.summary: なる means become: 暑くなる, get hot; 上手になる, get good. An adjective's く form on its own says how something's done: 大きく歌う, sing out loud.
grammar.body:
夏が、暑くなった。
歌が、上手になった。
今は、大きく歌える。
translations: Now I can sing out loud.

notes.text: An i-adjective swaps its い for く before なる: 暑い, 暑くなる. いい becomes よくなる.
A noun or a na-adjective takes に: 上手になる, 静かになる, 一つになる.
The same く form, with no なる after it, tells how something's done: 大きく (big, loud), 楽しく (happily), うまく (well).

grammar.title: ～みたい / ～そう
grammar.summary: みたい after a noun or a plain verb says it seems so: 雨みたい, sounds like rain. そう on an adjective's stem says how it looks: 怖そう, she looks scary.
grammar.body:
雨みたい。
リナ、怒ってるみたい。
リナさん、ちょっと怖そう。

notes.text: みたい is a guess from what you see or hear. It goes straight after a noun, or after the plain form of a verb or adjective: 怒ってるみたい, she seems angry.
Before a noun it's みたいな: 雨みたいな曲, a song like rain. In writing and formal talk it's ～ようだ.
そう goes on an adjective with its い dropped (怖い, 怖そう; 楽しい, 楽しそう) or on a verb's stem. It's how something looks to you, before you know. いい becomes よさそう.

grammar.title: ～ちゃう / ～てしまう
grammar.summary: しまう after a verb's て form says it's done and over, often when you didn't want it: 切れてしまった, it went and snapped. Friends say ちゃう: 切れちゃった.
grammar.body:
切れちゃった。
歌、忘れちゃった。
私、緊張しちゃう。

notes.text: て plus しまう shrinks to ちゃう, and で plus しまう to じゃう: 忘れちゃう, 飲んじゃう. In the past, ちゃった and じゃった.
It's often a small "oops": it happened, and it can't be undone. It can also just say something's done completely, or can't be helped.
The full てしまう is for writing and polite talk: 切れてしまいました.

grammar.title: ～てみる
grammar.summary: みる after a verb's て form means do it and see how it goes: 歌ってみる, try singing it.
grammar.body:
歌ってみて。
言葉、書いてみた。
もう一回、やってみよう。

notes.text: It's the verb 見る (see), written in kana: do something, and see what happens.
みる changes like 見る: やってみた (I tried it), やってみよう (let's give it a go), 静かにしてみて (try it quieter).

grammar.title: だけ / しか
grammar.summary: だけ after a word means only that: 三曲だけ, just three songs. しか with a negative verb means the same, with a feeling of not enough: 三曲しかない, we've only got three songs.
grammar.body:
三曲しかない。
三曲だけ。
ステージは、一回だけ。
translations: We only get one go on the stage.

notes.text: しか always comes with a negative: しかない (there's only), しか知らない (only know). It says there should be more.
だけ just says that's all there is, with no complaint, and works with any verb: 一回だけ (only once), 俺だけ (only me).
それだけ, "that's all", ends what you have to say.
